def print_boxed_banner(
    title: str,
    border_char: str = "*",
    width: int | None = None,
    pad: int = 2,
) -> None:
    """
    Print a boxed banner around *title*.

    Parameters
    ----------
    title : str
        Text to appear inside the box.
    border_char : str, optional
        One‑character string used for the border. Default: '*'.
    width : int | None, optional
        Desired total width of the box (including the border characters).
        If None, the box width is calculated as
        len(title) + 2*pad + 2 (the two vertical borders).
        If a value is supplied and it is too small to contain the title,
        the function raises a ValueError.
    pad : int, optional
        Minimum number of spaces added on each side of the title.
        Ignored when *width* is supplied – the padding is then auto‑adjusted
        so the title is centered (extra space goes to the right).

    Returns
    -------
    None
        The function prints directly to stdout.
    """
    # ----- Sanity checks -------------------------------------------------
    if not isinstance(border_char, str) or len(border_char) != 1:
        raise ValueError("border_char must be a single character string")

    title_len = len(title)

    # If width is given, compute the padding needed to centre the title.
    if width is not None:
        min_needed = title_len + 2  # just the two border chars, no padding
        if width < min_needed:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Requested width {width} is too small for title "
                f"'{title}' (needs at least {min_needed})."
            )
        # Number of spaces available _inside_ the borders
        inner_space = width - 2
        # Center the title (extra space on the right)
        left_pad = (inner_space - title_len) // 2
        right_pad = inner_space - title_len - left_pad
    else:
        # No explicit width → use the supplied pad value.
        left_pad = right_pad = pad
        width = title_len + 2 * pad + 2

    # ----- Build the three lines -----------------------------------------
    top_bottom = border_char * width
    middle = (
        border_char
        + " " * left_pad
        + title
        + " " * right_pad
        + border_char
    )

    # ----- Print the box ---------------------------------------------------
    print(top_bottom)
    print(middle)
    print(top_bottom)

    min_width: int | None = None,
) -> None:
    """
    Print a boxed banner around *title*.

    Parameters
    ----------
    title : str
        Text that will appear centred inside the box.
    border : str, optional
        One‑character string used for the box border.  The default is "*".
    padding : int, optional
        Minimum number of blank spaces added on each side of *title*.
        (The final left/right padding may be larger if ``min_width`` forces a
        wider box.)  Default = 1.
    min_width : int | None, optional
        Minimum interior width of the box (i.e. the space *between* the
        vertical border characters).  If ``None`` the interior width is
        just enough to fit the title plus the requested ``padding``.
        ``min_width`` is useful when you want several boxes to line up
        with the same width.

    Returns
    -------
    None
        The function prints directly to ``stdout``.
    """
    if len(border) != 1:
        raise ValueError("`border` must be a single character")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1️⃣ Determine the interior width of the box
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    #   - start with the width needed for the title + the *requested* padding
    #   - enlarge it if the user asked for a larger ``min_width``
    needed = len(title) + 2 * padding

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2️⃣ Distribute any extra space evenly on the left / right side
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    extra = interior_width - len(title) - 2 * padding
    left_extra  = extra // 2          # floor division

    # Build the middle line (the one that actually contains the title)
    middle = (

        + " " * (padding + right_extra)
        + border

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    horizontal = border * (interior_width + 2)   # +2 for the side borders

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    print(horizontal)

from typing import Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple, Union


def allergen_conflict_warning(
    recipe_tags: Sequence[str],
    user_avoid: Sequence[str],
    *,
    prefix: str = "⚠️  This recipe contains:",
    separator: str = ", ",
    suffix: str = ". Please avoid it.",
) -> Union[str, None]:
    """
    Compare the allergen tags of a recipe with a user’s “avoid” list.

    Parameters
    ----------
    recipe_tags : Sequence[str]
        The allergens listed for the recipe (e.g. ``["dairy", "peanuts", "gluten"]``).
    user_avoid : Sequence[str]
        The allergens the user wants to stay away from (e.g. ``["gluten", "shellfish"]``).
    prefix : str, optional
        Text that will appear before the list of conflicts. Defaults to a warning emoji.
    separator : str, optional
        String used to join the conflict names. Defaults to a comma and space.
    suffix : str, optional
        Text that will appear after the list of conflicts.

    Returns
    -------
    str | None
        * A warning message that includes **all** intersecting allergens,
          formatted as ``{prefix} {conflict1}{separator}{conflict2}{suffix}``.
        * ``None`` if there is **no overlap** between the two collections.

    Notes
    -----
    * The comparison is **case‑insensitive** and ignores surrounding whitespace.
    * Duplicate entries in either input are collapsed automatically.
    * Empty strings or ``None`` entries are ignored.

    Example
    -------
    >>> warning = allergen_conflict_warning(
    ...     ["Dairy", "peanuts", "gluten"],
    ...     ["gluten", "shellfish"]
    ... )
    >>> print(warning)
    ⚠️  This recipe contains: gluten. Please avoid it.
    """
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    # Normalise both inputs to lower‑case, stripped strings and discard
    # empties.  Converting to `set` also removes duplicates automatically.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    def _clean(values: Iterable[str | None]) -> Set[str]:
        return {
            v.strip().lower()
            for v in values
            if isinstance(v, str) and v.strip()
        }

    recipe_set = _clean(recipe_tags)
    avoid_set = _clean(user_avoid)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    # Find the intersection; if there is none we simply return ``None``.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    conflicts = recipe_set & avoid_set
    if not conflicts:
        return None

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    # Produce a deterministic output order – alphabetical is a safe default.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    sorted_conflicts: List[str] = sorted(conflicts)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    # Assemble the final warning string.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    return f"{prefix} {separator.join(sorted_conflicts)}{suffix}"

from typing import Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple, Union


def allergen_conflict_warning(
    recipe_tags: Sequence[str],
    user_avoid: Sequence[str],
    *,
    prefix: str = "⚠️  This recipe contains:",
    separator: str = ", ",
    suffix: str = ". Please avoid it.",
) -> Union[str, None]:
    """
    Compare the allergen tags of a recipe with a user’s “avoid” list.

    Parameters
    ----------
    recipe_tags : Sequence[str]
        The allergens listed for the recipe (e.g. ``["dairy", "peanuts", "gluten"]``).
    user_avoid : Sequence[str]
        The allergens the user wants to stay away from (e.g. ``["gluten", "shellfish"]``).
    prefix : str, optional
        Text that will appear before the list of conflicts. Defaults to a warning emoji.
    separator : str, optional
        String used to join the conflict names. Defaults to a comma and space.
    suffix : str, optional
        Text that will appear after the list of conflicts.

    Returns
    -------
    str | None
        * A warning message that includes **all** intersecting allergens,
          formatted as ``{prefix} {conflict1}{separator}{conflict2}{suffix}``.
        * ``None`` if there is **no overlap** between the two collections.

    Notes
    -----
    * The comparison is **case‑insensitive** and ignores surrounding whitespace.
    * Duplicate entries in either input are collapsed automatically.
    * Empty strings or ``None`` entries are ignored.

    Example
    -------
    >>> warning = allergen_conflict_warning(
    ...     ["Dairy", "peanuts", "gluten"],
    ...     ["gluten", "shellfish"]
    ... )
    >>> print(warning)
    ⚠️  This recipe contains: gluten. Please avoid it.
    """
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    # Normalise both inputs to lower‑case, stripped strings and discard
    # empties.  Converting to `set` also removes duplicates automatically.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    def _clean(values: Iterable[str | None]) -> Set[str]:
        return {
            v.strip().lower()
            for v in values
            if isinstance(v, str) and v.strip()
        }

    recipe_set = _clean(recipe_tags)
    avoid_set = _clean(user_avoid)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    # Find the intersection; if there is none we simply return ``None``.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    conflicts = recipe_set & avoid_set
    if not conflicts:
        return None

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    # Produce a deterministic output order – alphabetical is a safe default.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    sorted_conflicts: List[str] = sorted(conflicts)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    # Assemble the final warning string.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    return f"{prefix} {separator.join(sorted_conflicts)}{suffix}"

We’ll write a tiny utility called `receipt()` that builds a plain‑text receipt for a payment.  
The receipt must contain:

| Field   | Description                                 |
|---------|---------------------------------------------|
| payer   | Who is sending the money                    |
| payee   | Who is receiving the money                  |
| amount  | Numeric amount – formatted as a currency    |
| note    | Optional free‑form note (defaults to “‑”)   |

The function should be simple enough to drop into any project (no external libs required) and customizable enough for later extensions (e.g., different date formats, currencies, etc.).

---

## Code

```python
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Union

def receipt(
    payer: str,
    payee: str,
    amount: Union[int, float, str],
    note: str = "-",
    *,
    currency: str = "$",
    date: Union[datetime, str, None] = None,
    width: int = 40,
) -> str:
    """
    Build a formatted receipt string.

    Parameters
    ----------
    payer : str
        Name (or identifier) of the person sending the money.
    payee : str
        Name (or identifier) of the person receiving the money.
    amount : int | float | str
        The amount being transferred.  Numbers will be formatted with
        two decimal places; strings are used verbatim.
    note : str, optional
        Free‑form note.  If omitted, a single dash ("-") is placed.
    currency : str, optional (default='$')
        Currency symbol or code to prepend/append to the amount.
    date : datetime | str | None, optional
        Date of the transaction.  If ``None`` the current local date
        is used.  A ``datetime`` instance is formatted as ``YYYY‑MM‑DD``.
        A string is used as‑is.
    width : int, optional (default=40)
        Total width of the receipt; lines are left‑justified and padded
        to this width for a tidy block‑quote appearance.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        A multi‑line receipt ready to be printed, emailed, or stored.
    """
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1️⃣ Normalise the amount
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    if isinstance(amount, (int, float)):
        # Show two decimal places, thousands separators, e.g. $1,234.56
        amount_str = f"{currency}{amount:,.2f}"
    else:
        # Assume caller knows what they want (e.g. "$1,234")
        amount_str = f"{currency}{amount}"

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2️⃣ Normalise the date
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    if date is None:
        date_str = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    elif isinstance(date, datetime):
        date_str = date.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    else:
        date_str = str(date)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3️⃣ Build each line, padded to ``width``
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    lines = [
        f"{'RECEIPT':^{width}}",            # centered title
        "-" * width,
        f"Payer : {payer}",
        f"Payee : {payee}",
        f"Date  : {date_str}",
        f"Amount: {amount_str}",
        f"Note  : {note}",
        "-" * width,
        "Thank you for your business!",
    ]

    # Pad the short lines so the block looks rectangular
    padded = [ln.ljust(width) if len(ln) < width else ln for ln in lines]

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4️⃣ Return the full receipt as a single string
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    return "\n".join(padded)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example usage
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(receipt("Alice", "Bob", 1234.5, note="Invoice #987"))
    print()
    print(receipt("John Doe", "Acme Corp.", "2,500"))
```

---

## What the function does, step‑by‑step

| Step | Action | Reason |
|------|--------|--------|
| 1️⃣ | **Normalise the amount** – if a number is given we format it with two decimal places, thousands separators, and prepend the currency symbol. | Guarantees a consistent money format. |
| 2️⃣ | **Normalise the date** – default to *today*; accept a `datetime` object or a raw string. | Gives a timestamp without extra effort. |
| 3️⃣ | **Compose lines** – title, separator, payer/payee/etc., another separator, and a friendly footer. | Human‑readable layout, easy to scan. |
| 4️⃣ | **Pad lines** to a common width (`width` argument) – makes the receipt look like a block, ideal for plain‑text emails or logs. | Improves visual alignment. |
| 5️⃣ | **Return** a single string with new‑line characters. | Caller can `print()` it, write to a file, or embed in a message. |

---

## Customisation Hooks

- **Currency** – change `currency="€"` or `"USD "` if you want a trailing code.
- **Date format** – replace `strftime("%Y-%m-%d")` with any format you like.
- **Width** – make the receipt narrower/wider for different display contexts.
- **Additional fields** – simply add more entries to `lines` (e.g. `Transaction ID`, `Method`).  

Because the function returns a plain string, you can also post‑process it (e.g., add ANSI colour codes for terminal output).

---

----------------------------------------
Thank you for your business!

----------------------------------------

----------------------------------------
Thank you for your business!           
```

"""
path_normalizer.py

Utility for normalising user supplied file‑system style paths.

Features
--------
* Collapse any number of consecutive slashes ("/") into a single slash.
* Strip a trailing slash – **except** when the result would be an empty string,
  in which case we keep the root marker ("/").
* Return a fallback root marker ("/") when the input is blank, consists only
  of whitespace, or is `None`.

The implementation does not depend on `os.path.normpath` because that
function also collapses “..” and “.” components, which may be undesirable for a
pure “clean‑up” operation.  The code works on any POSIX‑style path string;
if you need Windows support (``\`` back‑slashes) you can replace the separator
character or easily extend the logic.

Example
-------
>>> normalize_path('///foo//bar///')
'/foo/bar'
>>> normalize_path('  ')
'/'
>>> normalize_path('C:/temp//')
'C:/temp'
>>> normalize_path('')
'/'
>>> normalize_path('/')
'/'
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Optional


def normalize_path(path: Optional[str]) -> str:
    """
    Collapse repeated slashes, remove a trailing slash, and fall back to '/'.

    Parameters
    ----------
    path : str or None
        The user‑supplied path.  ``None`` and any string that evaluates to
        *empty* after stripping whitespace are treated as a request for the
        root marker.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        A canonicalised path string.

    Notes
    -----
    * The function works on *POSIX* style paths (separator = "/").
    * It does **not** perform any filesystem checks – it only manipulates the
      textual representation.
    * Leading slashes are preserved (so ``///foo`` becomes ``/foo``).
    * If the resulting path would be empty, ``"/"`` is returned.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> normalize_path('///foo//bar///')
    '/foo/bar'
    >>> normalize_path('C:/temp//')
    'C:/temp'
    >>> normalize_path('')       # blank input → fallback root
    '/'
    >>> normalize_path(None)     # ``None`` is treated the same way
    '/'
    >>> normalize_path('/a/b/')  # trailing slash removed
    '/a/b'
    >>> normalize_path('/')      # root stays root
    '/'
    """
    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #
    # 1️⃣  Guard‑clause: treat ``None`` or “blank” input as a request for the
    #      fallback root marker.
    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #
    if path is None:
        return "/"

    # Strip whitespace first – a string containing only spaces should also be
    # considered “blank”.
    stripped = path.strip()
    if not stripped:
        return "/"

    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #
    # 2️⃣  Split on the slash separator, filter out empty parts (which collapse
    #      repeated slashes), then re‑join with a single slash.
    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #
    parts = [p for p in stripped.split("/") if p]  # drops '' → collapse

    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #
    # 3️⃣  Preserve a leading slash **iff** the original path started with one.
    #      (This keeps absolute paths absolute.)
    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #
    leading_slash = stripped.startswith("/")

    # Rebuild the path.
    normalised = "/" + "/".join(parts) if leading_slash else "/".join(parts)

    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #
    # 4️⃣  Remove a trailing slash, but *only* if the result would not become
    #      an empty string.  The root marker "/" must stay as is.
    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #
    if len(normalised) > 1 and normalised.endswith("/"):
        normalised = normalised[:-1]

    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #
    # 5️⃣  Edge case – when everything was stripped away (e.g. input was just
    #      "////") we end up with an empty string.  Return the fallback root.
    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #
    return normalised or "/"


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Simple sanity‑check when the module is executed directly.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
if __name__ == "__main__":
    import doctest
    doctest.testmod(verbose=True)

| **2️⃣ Collapse slashes** | `path.split("/")` → list of components → drop empty strings (`if p`) | Multiple consecutive slashes become a single separator. |
| **3️⃣ Preserve leading slash** | Detect `path.startswith("/")`.  If true, prepend `/` after joining. | Keeps absolute paths absolute. |
| **4️⃣ Trim trailing slash** | Remove a final “/” **unless** the result would be empty (`len>1`). | Normalises “/foo/” to “/foo”. |
| **5️⃣ Final fallback** | If after all processing we have `""` (happens for inputs like `"///"`), return `"/"`. | Guarantees we never return an empty string. |

-------

'/foo/bar'
>>> normalize_path('  ')
'/'
>>> normalize_path('C:/temp//')
'C:/temp'
>>> normalize_path('')
'/'
>>> normalize_path('/')
'/'

    --------

    '/'

    '/'
    >>> normalize_path('/a/b/')  # trailing slash removed
    '/a/b'
    >>> normalize_path('/')      # root stays root
    '/'

    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #

    # --------------------------------------------------------------------- #

    payee : str

    amount : Decimal | str | float | int

        but a string/float/int is also allowed for convenience.

    ------

    """

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    if not isinstance(amount, Decimal):

        untouched.

    strip_trailing:
        When ``True`` (default) removes a trailing separator, unless the
        whole string consists of a single separator.

    '/'

    '/foo/bar'
    >>> normalize_path('   ')
    '/'
    >>> normalize_path('', root_marker='.')
    '.'
    >>> normalize_path('C:\\\\Windows\\\\', collapse_multiple=False)
    'C:\\\\Windows\\\\'

    3. **Return a fallback** (``root_marker``) if the final result is an

    path:

        as “blank”.

        otherwise be empty.  The default value ``'/'`` works for typical
        POSIX‑style paths.

        into a single ``/``.  Set to ``False`` to keep the original string
        untouched.

    '/'

    '/'

1. **Account holder name** – a free‑form string (e.g., `"Jane Doe"`).
2. **Masked account number** – the original account number is kept only for the last 4 digits; all preceding digits are replaced with `*`.

   The function should work with any length of numeric account id (most common US accounts are 12‑16 digits, but the implementation does not assume a fixed length).
3. **Statement period** – a free‑form string that describes the date range (e.g., `"01/01/2023 – 01/31/2023"`).

All three parts are concatenated with `" | "` (pipe + spaces) as the separator.

The implementation is deliberately simple, well‑documented, and type‑annotated so that it can be dropped into any codebase or reused in unit tests.

## Implementation

```python
from __future__ import annotations

import re
from typing import Iterable


def mask_account_number(account_number: str, mask_char: str = "*") -> str:
    """
    Return a masked version of an account number, keeping only the last four digits.

    The mask replaces every digit **except** the final four with ``mask_char``
    and inserts a space after every four characters for readability, mimicking
    the common "#### #### #### 1234" layout.

    Parameters
    ----------
    account_number:
        The raw account number. It may contain digits, spaces or dashes.
        Non‑digit characters are ignored for the purposes of masking but are
        preserved (except dashes, which are stripped out).
    mask_char:
        Character used to replace hidden digits (default ``"*"``, can be any
        single‑character string).

    Returns
    -------
    str
        A string like ``"**** **** 1234"`` or ``"**** **** **** 5678"``.
    """
    # Keep only numeric characters – everything else is ignored.
    digits = re.sub(r"\D", "", account_number)

    # If the account number is 4 digits or less we expose it entirely.
    if len(digits) <= 4:
        return digits

    # Build the masked string: all but the last four become mask_char.
    hidden_part = mask_char * (len(digits) - 4)
    visible_part = digits[-4:]
    masked = hidden_part + visible_part

    # Insert a space every 4 characters for readability.
    # Example: "********1234" -> "**** **** 1234"
    groups: Iterable[str] = (masked[i : i + 4] for i in range(0, len(masked), 4))
    return " ".join(groups)


def format_statement_header(
    holder_name: str,
    account_number: str,
    statement_period: str,
    separator: str = " | ",
) -> str:
    """
    Build a pipe‑separated statement header.

    Parameters
    ----------
    holder_name:
        Full name of the account holder.
    account_number:
        Raw account number (may contain spaces/dashes). It will be masked.
    statement_period:
        Human‑readable period (e.g. ``"01/01/2023 – 01/31/2023"``).
    separator:
        Token placed between the three fields. Defaults to ``" | "``.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        Header ready for printing or inclusion in a PDF/HTML report, e.g.

        ``"Jane Doe | **** **** 1234 | 01/01/2023 – 01/31/2023"``
    """
    masked_number = mask_account_number(account_number)
    # Strip surrounding whitespace from each component to avoid accidental double spaces.
    parts = [holder_name.strip(), masked_number.strip(), statement_period.strip()]
    return separator.join(parts)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Example usage (run directly from the module):
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example data
    name = "Jane Doe"
    acct = "1234-5678-9012-3456"
    period = "01/01/2023 – 01/31/2023"

    header = format_statement_header(name, acct, period)
    print(header)  # → Jane Doe | **** **** **** 3456 | 01/01/2023 – 01/31/2023
```

### How It Works

1. **`mask_account_number`**
   * Strips all non‑digit characters (`re.sub(r"\D", "", ...)`) – this normalises inputs like `"1234 5678 9012"` or `"1234-5678-9012"`.
   * If the number has ≤ 4 digits we simply return it (nothing to mask).
   * Otherwise we create a string of `mask_char` repeated for every digit except the last four, concatenate the visible suffix, and finally inject a space every four characters for readability.

2. **`format_statement_header`**
   * Calls `mask_account_number` to obtain the masked representation.
   * Trims whitespace from each piece.
   * Joins the three strings using the supplied separator (default `" | "`).

Both functions are tiny, have **O(n)** time complexity (where *n* is the length of the account number string), and **O(1)** extra space aside from the output string.

**Solution Overview**

We need a small utility that builds a bank‑statement header string consisting of three parts:

1. **Account holder name** – a free‑form string (e.g., `"Jane Doe"`).
2. **Masked account number** – the original account number is kept only for the last 4 digits; all preceding digits are replaced with `*`.  
   For readability we keep the familiar “group‑of‑4” spacing (e.g., `**** **** 1234`).  
   The function should work with any length of numeric account id (most common US accounts are 12‑16 digits, but the implementation does not assume a fixed length).
3. **Statement period** – a free‑form string that describes the date range (e.g., `"01/01/2023 – 01/31/2023"`).

All three parts are concatenated with `" | "` (pipe + spaces) as the separator.

The implementation is deliberately simple, well‑documented, and type‑annotated so that it can be dropped into any codebase or reused in unit tests.

---

## Implementation

```python
from __future__ import annotations

import re
from typing import Iterable


def mask_account_number(account_number: str, mask_char: str = "*") -> str:
    """
    Return a masked version of an account number, keeping only the last four digits.

    The mask replaces every digit **except** the final four with ``mask_char``
    and inserts a space after every four characters for readability, mimicking
    the common "#### #### #### 1234" layout.

    Parameters
    ----------
    account_number:
        The raw account number. It may contain digits, spaces or dashes.
        Non‑digit characters are ignored for the purposes of masking but are
        preserved (except dashes, which are stripped out).
    mask_char:
        Character used to replace hidden digits (default ``"*"``, can be any
        single‑character string).

    Returns
    -------
    str
        A string like ``"**** **** 1234"`` or ``"**** **** **** 5678"``.
    """
    # Keep only numeric characters – everything else is ignored.
    digits = re.sub(r"\D", "", account_number)

    # If the account number is 4 digits or less we expose it entirely.
    if len(digits) <= 4:
        return digits

    # Build the masked string: all but the last four become mask_char.
    hidden_part = mask_char * (len(digits) - 4)
    visible_part = digits[-4:]
    masked = hidden_part + visible_part

    # Insert a space every 4 characters for readability.
    # Example: "********1234" -> "**** **** 1234"
    groups: Iterable[str] = (masked[i : i + 4] for i in range(0, len(masked), 4))
    return " ".join(groups)


def format_statement_header(
    holder_name: str,
    account_number: str,
    statement_period: str,
    separator: str = " | ",
) -> str:
    """
    Build a pipe‑separated statement header.

    Parameters
    ----------
    holder_name:
        Full name of the account holder.
    account_number:
        Raw account number (may contain spaces/dashes). It will be masked.
    statement_period:
        Human‑readable period (e.g. ``"01/01/2023 – 01/31/2023"``).
    separator:
        Token placed between the three fields. Defaults to ``" | "``.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        Header ready for printing or inclusion in a PDF/HTML report, e.g.

        ``"Jane Doe | **** **** 1234 | 01/01/2023 – 01/31/2023"``
    """
    masked_number = mask_account_number(account_number)
    # Strip surrounding whitespace from each component to avoid accidental double spaces.
    parts = [holder_name.strip(), masked_number.strip(), statement_period.strip()]
    return separator.join(parts)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Example usage (run directly from the module):
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example data
    name = "Jane Doe"
    acct = "1234-5678-9012-3456"
    period = "01/01/2023 – 01/31/2023"

    header = format_statement_header(name, acct, period)
    print(header)  # → Jane Doe | **** **** **** 3456 | 01/01/2023 – 01/31/2023
```

### How It Works

1. **`mask_account_number`**
   * Strips all non‑digit characters (`re.sub(r"\D", "", ...)`) – this normalises inputs like `"1234 5678 9012"` or `"1234-5678-9012"`.
   * If the number has ≤ 4 digits we simply return it (nothing to mask).
   * Otherwise we create a string of `mask_char` repeated for every digit except the last four, concatenate the visible suffix, and finally inject a space every four characters for readability.

2. **`format_statement_header`**
   * Calls `mask_account_number` to obtain the masked representation.
   * Trims whitespace from each piece.
   * Joins the three strings using the supplied separator (default `" | "`).

Both functions are tiny, have **O(n)** time complexity (where *n* is the length of the account number string), and **O(1)** extra space aside from the output string.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

"""
ext2category.py – Simple utility that maps file extensions to category labels.

Features
--------
* 1‑line public API: :func:`extension_to_category(ext_or_path)`.
* Handles extensions with or without a leading period (".txt", "txt").
* Accepts either a raw extension *or* a full file‑path string.
* Returns a sensible default label – "Unknown" – for anything it does not know.
* Extensible: add new extensions to the ``_EXTENSION_MAP`` dictionary.

Example
-------
>>> from ext2category import extension_to_category
>>> extension_to_category("photo.JPG")
'Image'
>>> extension_to_category("/tmp/report.pdf")
'Document'
>>> extension_to_category("archive.7z")
'Archive'
>>> extension_to_category("somefile.xyz")
'Unknown'
"""

import os
import sys
from typing import Dict

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Mapping of extensions (lower‑case, without leading dot) to category labels.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
_EXTENSION_MAP: Dict[str, str] = {
    # ---- Images ----------------------------------------------------------- #
    "jpg": "Image",
    "jpeg": "Image",
    "png": "Image",
    "gif": "Image",
    "bmp": "Image",
    "tif": "Image",
    "tiff": "Image",
    "webp": "Image",
    "svg": "Image",
    "heic": "Image",
    # ---- Documents -------------------------------------------------------- #
    "pdf": "Document",
    "doc": "Document",
    "docx": "Document",
    "odt": "Document",
    "rtf": "Document",
    "txt": "Document",
    "md": "Document",
    "tex": "Document",
    "ppt": "Document",
    "pptx": "Document",
    "xls": "Document",
    "xlsx": "Document",
    # ---- Archives ---------------------------------------------------------- #
    "zip": "Archive",
    "tar": "Archive",
    "gz": "Archive",
    "bz2": "Archive",
    "xz": "Archive",
    "7z": "Archive",
    "rar": "Archive",
    # ---- Audio ------------------------------------------------------------ #
    "mp3": "Audio",
    "wav": "Audio",
    "flac": "Audio",
    "aac": "Audio",
    "ogg": "Audio",
    "m4a": "Audio",
    # ---- Video ------------------------------------------------------------ #
    "mp4": "Video",
    "avi": "Video",
    "mkv": "Video",
    "mov": "Video",
    "wmv": "Video",
    "webm": "Video",
    # ---- Code / Scripts ---------------------------------------------------- #
    "py": "Code",
    "js": "Code",
    "ts": "Code",
    "java": "Code",
    "c": "Code",
    "cpp": "Code",
    "cs": "Code",
    "rb": "Code",
    "go": "Code",
    "php": "Code",
    "html": "Code",
    "css": "Code",
    "sql": "Code",
    # ---- Misc ------------------------------------------------------------- #
    "json": "Data",
    "csv": "Data",
    "xml": "Data",
    "yml": "Data",
    "yaml": "Data",
}


def _normalise_ext(ext: str) -> str:
    """Return a lower‑cased extension without any leading dot.

    Parameters
    ----------
    ext: str
        Extension string possibly starting with '.' (e.g. ".JPG").

    Returns
    -------
    str
        Normalised extension (e.g. "jpg").
    """
    return ext.lower().lstrip(".")


def extension_to_category(ext_or_path: str) -> str:
    """Map a filename or a bare extension to a category label.

    The function extracts the extension (if a path is supplied), normalises it,
    and looks it up in the internal mapping table.

    Parameters
    ----------
    ext_or_path : str
        Either:
        * a full file name / path ("folder/image.PNG"),
        * or just an extension ("png" or ".png").

    Returns
    -------
    str
        Human‑readable category. Returns "Unknown" when the extension is not
        recognised.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> extension_to_category("picture.jpg")
    'Image'
    >>> extension_to_category(".pdf")
    'Document'
    >>> extension_to_category("/tmp/archive.tar.gz")
    'Archive'
    >>> extension_to_category("unknown.xyz")
    'Unknown'
    """
    # If the string looks like a path, extract its extension.
    # ``os.path.splitext`` splits at the last dot only, which is exactly what
    # we want for simple cases. For compound extensions like ".tar.gz" we treat
    # the whole thing as the extension – the mapping contains "gz" which maps
    # to "Archive", so it works.
    _, ext = os.path.splitext(ext_or_path)
    # ``os.path.splitext`` returns '' when there is no dot in the input,
    # causing ``_normalise_ext`` to return ''.
    # In that case we assume the user passed a bare extension (e.g. "pdf").
    if not ext:
        ext = ext_or_path

    norm = _normalise_ext(ext)

    # Lookup – default to "Unknown".
    return _EXTENSION_MAP.get(norm, "Unknown")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Simple CLI for quick manual testing
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def _cli():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        prog = os.path.basename(sys.argv[0])
        print(f"Usage: {prog} <file-or-extension> [<file-or-extension> ...]")
        sys.exit(1)

    for arg in sys.argv[1:]:
        label = extension_to_category(arg)
        print(f"{arg!r:30} → {label}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    _cli()
```

## How to Use

```python
from ext2category import extension_to_category

# Pass a full path
print(extension_to_category("/home/user/photo.jpeg"))   # → "Image"

# Pass only an extension (dot optional)
print(extension_to_category(".pdf"))                  # → "Document"
print(extension_to_category("zip"))                   # → "Archive"

# Unknown / unsupported
print(extension_to_category("myfile.xyz"))            # → "Unknown"
```

## Extending the Mapping

The public constant `_EXTENSION_MAP` lives near the top of the file.  
To add a new type, simply insert another key/value pair:

```python
_EXTENSION_MAP["psd"] = "Image"      # Photoshop document
_EXTENSION_MAP["epub"] = "Document" # e‑book
```

After editing, re‑run your code – the change takes effect immediately.

        self.assertEqual(extension_to_category("notes.md"), "Document")

    """Return a lower‑cased extension without any leading dot.

    ----------

    Returns

def extension_to_category(ext_or_path: str) -> str:
    """Map a filename or a bare extension to a category label.

    The function extracts the extension (if a path is supplied), normalises it,
    and looks it up in the internal mapping table.

    Parameters
    ----------
    ext_or_path : str

    # we want for simple cases. For compound extensions like ".tar.gz" we treat
    # the whole thing as the extension – the mapping contains "gz" which maps

    if not ext:

Usage
-----
>>> headers = ["Product", "Units Sold", "Revenue", "Margin%"]

"""

from typing import List, Any


def _is_number(value: Any) -> bool:
    """Return True if ``value`` should be treated as a numeric field.

    Numbers (int, float, Decimal) and strings that consist **only** of
    digits, a leading sign, a decimal point, or a trailing `%` are
    considered numeric for alignment purposes.
    """
    if isinstance(value, (int, float)):
        return True
    if isinstance(value, str):
        s = value.strip()
        # Allow leading sign, decimal point, percent sign, or commas
        s = s.replace(",", "")
        if s.endswith("%"):
            s = s[:-1]
        try:
            float(s)
            return True
        except ValueError:
            return False
    return False


class SalesSummaryTable:
    """
    Render a plain‑text table with a header row, aligned columns, and a
    divider line made of dashes (or any characters you choose).

    Parameters
    ----------
    headers : list of str
        Column headings.
    rows : list of list
        Each inner list represents one row of data; its length must match
        ``len(headers)``.
    corner : str, optional
        Character used at the intersection of vertical and horizontal
        lines (default ``'+'``).
    hline : str, optional
        Horizontal line character (default ``'-'``).
    vline : str, optional
        Vertical line character (default ``'|'``).
    padding : int, optional
        Number of spaces added on *both* sides of a cell (default 1).
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        headers: List[str],
        rows: List[List[Any]],
        *,
        corner: str = "+",
        hline: str = "-",
        vline: str = "|",
        padding: int = 1,
    ) -> None:
        if any(len(row) != len(headers) for row in rows):
            raise ValueError("All rows must have the same number of columns as the header.")

        self.headers = list(headers)
        self.rows = [list(r) for r in rows]
        self.corner = corner
        self.hline = hline
        self.vline = vline
        self.padding = padding

        # Compute column widths once – they never change after init.
        self._col_widths = self._compute_column_widths()

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    # Internal helpers
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    def _compute_column_widths(self) -> List[int]:
        """
        Determine the width of each column based on header & cell contents.
        The width includes the *content* only; the surrounding padding
        (``self.padding``) is added later when rendering.
        """
        # start with the header lengths
        col_widths = [len(str(h)) for h in self.headers]

        # compare with each cell in all rows
        for row in self.rows:
            for idx, cell in enumerate(row):
                cell_len = len(str(cell))
                if cell_len > col_widths[idx]:
                    col_widths[idx] = cell_len
        return col_widths

    def _make_divider(self) -> str:
        """Construct a line such as ``+-----+-------+``."""
        parts = [self.corner]
        for width in self._col_widths:
            # width + 2*padding spaces = total interior width
            parts.append(self.hline * (width + 2 * self.padding))
            parts.append(self.corner)
        return "".join(parts)

    def _format_cell(self, content: Any, width: int, align_right: bool) -> str:
        """
        Return a cell string padded with spaces, ready to be placed
        between vertical borders.
        """
        txt = str(content)
        if align_right:
            padded = txt.rjust(width)
        else:
            padded = txt.ljust(width)
        # add left/right padding spaces
        return " " * self.padding + padded + " " * self.padding

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    # Public API
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    def render(self) -> str:
        """Return the full table as a single string."""
        lines = []

        # top border
        lines.append(self._make_divider())

        # header row
        header_cells = [
            self._format_cell(h, w, align_right=False)
            for h, w in zip(self.headers, self._col_widths)
        ]
        lines.append(self.vline + self.vline.join(header_cells) + self.vline)

        # separator under header
        lines.append(self._make_divider())

        # data rows
        for row in self.rows:
            row_cells = []
            for cell, width in zip(row, self._col_widths):
                right = _is_number(cell)
                row_cells.append(self._format_cell(cell, width, align_right=right))
            lines.append(self.vline + self.vline.join(row_cells) + self.vline)

        # bottom border
        lines.append(self._make_divider())

        return "\n".join(lines)

    # The dunder method makes ``print(table)`` work out‑of‑the‑box.
    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return self.render()

"""authorization_helpers.py

Utility for safely parsing an HTTP ``Authorization`` header.

The public API consists of a single function:

    parse_authorization_header(value: str) -> tuple[str, str]

It returns ``(scheme, credential)`` or ``("", "")`` when the input cannot be
interpreted as a valid Authorization header.

Typical usage:

    >>> parse_authorization_header("Bearer   abc123")
    ('Bearer', 'abc123')
    >>> parse_authorization_header("Basic")
    ('', '')
    >>> parse_authorization_header(None)
    ('', '')
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Tuple


def parse_authorization_header(value: str | None) -> Tuple[str, str]:
    """
    Split an ``Authorization`` header into its scheme and credential parts.

    Parameters
    ----------
    value : str or None
        The raw ``Authorization`` header value as received from the request.
        ``None`` (or any non‑string) is treated as a missing/invalid header.

    Returns
    -------
    tuple[str, str]
        ``(scheme, credential)`` when the header looks like ``"<scheme> <credential>"``.
        If the header is empty, malformed, or does not contain a space separating
        the two parts, the function returns ``("", "")``.

    Notes
    -----
    * Leading and trailing whitespace are ignored.
    * The split is performed **once**, i.e. only the *first* whitespace separates
      the scheme from the credential.  Any additional whitespace is considered
      part of the credential.
    * The function does **not** validate the credential (e.g. Base64 decoding);
      it only checks that both components are non‑empty after stripping.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> parse_authorization_header("Bearer   abcdef")
    ('Bearer', 'abcdef')
    >>> parse_authorization_header("Basic QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==")
    ('Basic', 'QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==')
    >>> parse_authorization_header("MalformedHeader")
    ('', '')
    >>> parse_authorization_header("")
    ('', '')
    >>> parse_authorization_header(None)
    ('', '')
    """
    # Guard against ``None`` or non‑string input.
    if not isinstance(value, str):
        return "", ""

    # Strip surrounding whitespace – it is not significant for the format.
    trimmed = value.strip()
    if not trimmed:
        return "", ""

    # Split only on the first run of whitespace (space, tab, etc.).
    # ``maxsplit=1`` guarantees we keep the rest of the string (including extra
    # spaces) as part of the credential.
    parts = trimmed.split(None, 1)  # ``None`` makes it split on any whitespace.

    # A valid Authorization header must contain exactly two non‑empty parts.
    if len(parts) != 2:
        return "", ""

    scheme, credential = parts[0].strip(), parts[1].strip()

    # Both pieces have to be non‑empty after stripping.
    if not scheme or not credential:
        return "", ""

    return scheme, credential

import re

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Regular expression that works for the most common Java logging patterns.
#
# Typical patterns:
#   2023-10-01 12:34:56,789 [main] INFO  com.example.MyClass - Hello world
#   10:15:42,123 [http-nio-8080-exec-1] DEBUG - Starting request
#   2023‑01‑01 00:00:00,000 WARN  - Something went wrong
#
# Explanation of the groups:
#   1 – optional timestamp (ignored)
#   2 – optional thread name inside [...]
#   3 – optional log level (INFO|DEBUG|WARN|ERROR|TRACE|FATAL|SEVERE)
#   4 – the actual message (everything after the first dash)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
_LOG_LINE_RE = re.compile(
    r"""
    ^                                 # start of line
    (?:\S+\s+\S+(?:,\d+)?)?           # optional timestamp (e.g. 2023-10-01 12:34:56,789)
    \s*                               # optional whitespace
    (?:\[(?P<thread>[^\]]+)\])?       # optional thread name in [...]
    \s*                               # optional whitespace
    (?P<level>INFO|DEBUG|WARN|ERROR|TRACE|FATAL|SEVERE)?   # optional log level
    (?:\s+[\w\.]+)?                   # optional logger name (ignored)
    \s*-\s*                           # dash that separates the header from the message
    (?P<msg>.*)                       # the actual log message (can be empty)
    $                                 # end of line
    """,
    re.IGNORECASE | re.VERBOSE,
)


def parse_java_log_line(line: str) -> Dict[str, str]:
    """
    Extract ``level``, ``thread`` and ``message`` from a Java log line.

    Parameters
    ----------
    line:
        The raw log line as a *single* string (including newline characters if any).

    Returns
    -------
    dict
        ``{'level': <level>, 'thread': <thread>, 'message': <msg>}``.  Any missing part
        is represented by an empty string (``''``).

    Notes
    -----
    * The function is deliberately tolerant – if the line does **not** match the
      expected pattern, all three fields are returned as empty strings.
    * The regex is case‑insensitive for the level, so ``INFO`` and ``info`` are both
      accepted.
    * A missing *thread* or *level* does **not** prevent the *message* from being
      captured.
    """
    if not isinstance(line, str):
        raise TypeError("log line must be a string")

    match = _LOG_LINE_RE.match(line.strip())
    if not match:
        # Nothing could be parsed – return empty values.
        return {"level": "", "thread": "", "message": ""}

    # ``groupdict`` gives keys for each named capture group.
    # Missing groups are ``None`` – we coerce them to ``''``.
    result = {k: (v or "") for k, v in match.groupdict().items()}

|-------------------|----------------|-------------------|

"""
file_category.py – Map a file extension to a human‑readable category.

Typical usage
-------------
>>> from file_category import categorize
>>> categorize("photo.JPG")

>>> categorize("report.pdf")

>>> categorize("archive.tar.gz")

>>> categorize("random.xyz")

import os
import sys
from typing import Final, Mapping

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 1.   The extension → category mapping
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

# NOTE: All keys are lower‑case and **without** the leading dot.
# Add more extensions as you need them – the dictionary is deliberately kept
# simple so that it can be exported/imported easily.
_EXTENSION_MAP: Final[Mapping[str, str]] = {
    # ────── Images ──────
    "png": "image",
    "jpg": "image",
    "jpeg": "image",
    "gif": "image",
    "bmp": "image",
    "tiff": "image",
    "webp": "image",
    "svg": "image",
    "heic": "image",
    # ────── Documents ──────
    "pdf": "document",
    "doc": "document",
    "docx": "document",
    "txt": "document",
    "rtf": "document",
    "odt": "document",
    "md": "document",
    "xls": "document",
    "xlsx": "document",
    "csv": "document",
    "ppt": "document",
    "pptx": "document",
    # ────── Archives ──────
    "zip": "archive",
    "tar": "archive",
    "gz": "archive",
    "bz2": "archive",
    "xz": "archive",
    "rar": "archive",
    "7z": "archive",
    "tgz": "archive",
    "tbz": "archive",
    # ────── Audio ──────
    "mp3": "audio",
    "wav": "audio",
    "flac": "audio",
    "aac": "audio",
    "ogg": "audio",
    # ────── Video ──────
    "mp4": "video",
    "avi": "video",
    "mkv": "video",
    "mov": "video",
    "wmv": "video",
    "webm": "video",
    "flv": "video",
}
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def _normalize_extension(ext: str) -> str:
    """
    Normalise the raw extension string:

    * strip leading dots,
    * make lower‑case,
    * keep everything after the **last** dot only (e.g. “tar.gz” → “gz”).

    Args:
        ext: Raw extension (may contain a dot, may be part of a longer name).

    Returns:
        The cleaned extension, ready to be looked‑up in `_EXTENSION_MAP`.
    """
    # "my.archive.tar.gz" -> "gz"
    # keep only the part after the final '.' (commonsense for files like *.tar.gz)
    if not ext:
        return ""

    # If a filename is passed instead of just the suffix, split it first.
    # os.path.splitext works on full filenames, not on "gz".
    # >>> os.path.splitext("foo.tar.gz") => ('foo.tar', '.gz')
    # That's why we strip everything up to the first dot then keep the tail.
    # A simple rsplit is enough.
    ext = ext.rsplit(".", 1)[-1]  # keep tail after last dot

    # Strip any remaining leading dot (e.g. ".gz" → "gz")
    ext = ext.lstrip(".")

    return ext.lower()


def categorize(
    filename_or_ext: str,
    unknown_label: str = "unknown",
) -> str:
    """
    Return the category label for a given file name or extension.

    Parameters
    ----------
    filename_or_ext:
        Either a full filename (e.g. ``picture.JPG``) **or** just the extension
        (e.g. ``.pdf`` or ``pdf``). The function is tolerant to leading dots
        and to mixed case.

    unknown_label:
        The label to return when the extension is not present in the internal
        mapping.  Defaults to ``"unknown"``.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        One of the category strings defined in ``_EXTENSION_MAP`` or the
        ``unknown_label``.

    Example
    -------

    'image'

    'document'

    'archive'
    >>> categorize("somefile.xyz")
    'unknown'

    normalized = _normalize_extension(filename_or_ext)

    # Look up in the mapping – default to the unknown label.
    return _EXTENSION_MAP.get(normalized, unknown_label)

| Step | What happens | Code snippet |

| **1️⃣** | Accept either a *full filename* (`photo.jpg`) **or** a raw *extension* (`.tar.gz`). | The public `categorize()` function receives the user input. |
| **2️⃣** | Strip everything up to the **last** period, remove any leading dot, and lower‑case the result. | `_normalize_extension()` uses `rsplit(".", 1)` + `lstrip(".")`. |

>>> format_tags(None)
'no tags provided'

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Iterable, List, Sequence


def format_tags(
    tags: Sequence[str] | Iterable[str] | None,
    *,
    fallback: str = "no tags provided",
    joiner: str = ", ",
) -> str:
    """
    Convert a collection of tags into a nicely formatted string.

    Parameters
    ----------
    tags : Sequence[str] | Iterable[str] | None
        The collection of tags to format.  ``None`` or an empty collection
        triggers the ``fallback`` value.
    fallback : str, optional
        Text to return when ``tags`` is empty or ``None``.
        Default: ``"no tags provided"``.
    joiner : str, optional
        String used to join the individual tags.  Default is ``", "``.
        You can pass a different separator (e.g. ``" | "``, ``" - "``)
        without changing the fallback logic.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        A single string containing the tags joined by ``joiner`` or
        the ``fallback`` value if there are no tags.

    Raises
    ------
    TypeError
        If ``tags`` is not iterable (other than ``None``) or contains
        non‑string elements.
    """
    # --------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1️⃣ Normalise the input
    # --------------------------------------------------------------
    if tags is None:
        # Nothing to work with – return the fallback early.
        return fallback

    # Convert to a list so we can safely check length and iterate multiple
    # times without exhausting a generator.
    try:
        tag_list: List[str] = list(tags)   # type: ignore[arg-type]
    except TypeError as exc:
        raise TypeError("tags must be an iterable of strings or None") from exc

    # --------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2️⃣ Guard against empty collections
    # --------------------------------------------------------------
    if not tag_list:
        return fallback

    # --------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3️⃣ Validate element types (optional but nice for debugging)
    # --------------------------------------------------------------
    for i, tag in enumerate(tag_list):
        if not isinstance(tag, str):
            raise TypeError(
                f"All tags must be strings; element #{i} is a {type(tag)!r}"

    # 4️⃣ Produce the final string
    # --------------------------------------------------------------
    return joiner.join(tag_list)

import re
from typing import Mapping, Callable, Match


def replace_placeholders(
    template: str,
    values: Mapping[str, str],
    *,
    pattern: str = r'\b([A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*)\b',
    missing: Callable[[str], str] = lambda name: name,
) -> str:
    """
    Replace word‑style placeholders inside *template* with real values from *values*.

    Parameters
    ----------
    template:
        The configuration text (or any string) that may contain placeholders.
    values:
        Mapping from placeholder name → replacement string.
        For example: ``{'HOST': 'localhost', 'PORT': '8080'}``.
    pattern (optional):
        Regular‑expression pattern that identifies placeholders.
        The default ``r'\\b([A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*)\\b'`` matches a whole word that
        starts with a capital letter and contains only capital letters,
        digits or underscores (common for env‑style keys).
        Capture group 1 is the *name* that will be looked up in ``values``.
    missing (optional):
        Callable invoked when a placeholder is **not** found in ``values``.
        The default simply returns the placeholder unchanged (i.e. leaves it as‑is).
        You can use this hook to emit warnings, raise an error, or replace it with
        a default value.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        The resulting string with all known placeholders substituted.

    Example
    -------
    >>> tmpl = (
    ...     "server {{HOST}}:{{PORT}}\n"
    ...     "user = $DB_USER\n"
    ...     "password = $DB_PASS\n"
    ... )
    >>> # Switch the pattern to handle the double‑curly‑brace style:
    >>> replace_placeholders(
    ...     tmpl,
    ...     {'HOST': '127.0.0.1', 'PORT': '5000', 'DB_USER': 'admin'},
    ...     pattern=r'\\{\\{([A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*)\\}\\}|\\$([A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*)',
    ...     missing=lambda name: f'<<MISSING:{name}>>'
    ... )
    'server 127.0.0.1:5000\\nuser = admin\\npassword = <<MISSING:DB_PASS>>\\n'
    """
    # Compile once for speed, especially useful for big templates.
    regex = re.compile(pattern)

    def _replacer(match: Match[str]) -> str:
        # ``match`` can contain several capture groups (e.g. when the pattern
        # matches both {{NAME}} and $NAME).  The first non‑None group is the
        # placeholder's name.
        placeholder_name = next(
            (grp for grp in match.groups() if grp is not None), None
        )
        if placeholder_name is None:
            # Should never happen because the pattern guarantees at least one group.
            return match.group(0)

        if placeholder_name in values:
            # Convert the replacement to ``str`` in case the user passed ints,
            # booleans, etc.
            return str(values[placeholder_name])
        else:
            # Let the caller decide what to do with unknown placeholders.
            return missing(placeholder_name)

    return regex.sub(_replacer, template)

) -> str:

    "5 parts – top level: 'home'"

    >>> short_path_description(r"C:\\Windows\\System32")
    "3 parts – top level: 'Windows'"

    >>> short_path_description("")
    'No path provided'
    """

    # -------------------------------------------------
    # 1️⃣  Guard against “empty” input.
    # -------------------------------------------------

    # -------------------------------------------------

    #     pathlib.Path, os.PathLike objects uniformly).
    # -------------------------------------------------

    # -------------------------------------------------
    # 3️⃣  Strip any trailing separator – Path.parts already
    #     behaves nicely, but a path that ends with a separator
    #     like "foo/bar/" will still have the same parts count.
    # -------------------------------------------------
    # (no action needed – Path.parts works as‑is)

    # -------------------------------------------------

    # -------------------------------------------------

    #   ('C:\\', 'Windows', 'System32')    on Windows

    # so we subtract it from the human‑readable count.
    #

    #   ('\\\\', 'server', 'share', 'folder')
    #

    # -------------------------------------------------

    if n_parts == 0:

    # -------------------------------------------------
    # 6️⃣  Assemble the final sentence.
    # -------------------------------------------------
    # Use singular/plural grammar for “part(s)”.

import csv
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Iterable, Tuple


def load_events(csv_path: Path) -> Iterable[Tuple[str, str, str]]:
    """
    Yield (user, action, outcome) rows from a CSV file.
    Assumes a header row containing at least the columns:
        user, action, outcome
    """
    with csv_path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        for row in reader:
            # Normalise column names (strip spaces, lower‑case)
            user = row.get("user") or row.get("User") or ""
            action = row.get("action") or row.get("Action") or ""
            outcome = row.get("outcome") or row.get("Outcome") or ""
            yield user.strip(), action.strip(), outcome.strip()


def count_failed_actions(events: Iterable[Tuple[str, str, str]]) -> dict:
    """
    Return a mapping {user: failed_count}.
    """
    failures = defaultdict(int)
    for user, _action, outcome in events:
        if outcome.lower() == "failed":
            failures[user] += 1
    return dict(failures)


def build_report(failure_counts: dict) -> str:
    """
    Create a multi‑line report string.
    Each user line is followed by a line of dashes.
    Example:
        UserA – 5 failed actions
        -----
        UserB – 0 failed actions
        -----
    """
    if not failure_counts:
        return "No data found."

    # Sort users alphabetically (optional: sort by count, etc.)
    lines = []
    for user in sorted(failure_counts):
        lines.append(f"{user} – {failure_counts[user]} failed action{'s' if failure_counts[user] != 1 else ''}")
        lines.append("-----")
    # Remove the trailing separator if you don't want an extra line at the end
    if lines and lines[-1] == "-----":
        lines.pop()
    return "\n".join(lines)


def generate_failure_report(csv_file: str) -> str:
    """
    High‑level helper: read a CSV file, count failures, return the report string.
    """
    path = Path(csv_file)
    events = load_events(path)
    failures = count_failed_actions(events)
    return build_report(failures)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Path to your CSV export
    csv_path = "app_events.csv"

    report = generate_failure_report(csv_path)
    print(report)

def load_events(csv_path: Path) -> Iterable[Tuple[str, str, str]]:
    """
    Yield (user, action, outcome) rows from a CSV file.
    Assumes a header row containing at least the columns:
        user, action, outcome
    """
    with csv_path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        for row in reader:
            # Normalise column names (strip spaces, lower‑case)
            user = row.get("user") or row.get("User") or ""
            action = row.get("action") or row.get("Action") or ""
            outcome = row.get("outcome") or row.get("Outcome") or ""
            yield user.strip(), action.strip(), outcome.strip()


def count_failed_actions(events: Iterable[Tuple[str, str, str]]) -> dict:
    """
    Return a mapping {user: failed_count}.
    """
    failures = defaultdict(int)
    for user, _action, outcome in events:
        if outcome.lower() == "failed":
            failures[user] += 1
    return dict(failures)


def build_report(failure_counts: dict) -> str:
    """
    Create a multi‑line report string.
    Each user line is followed by a line of dashes.
    Example:
        UserA – 5 failed actions
        -----
        UserB – 0 failed actions
        -----
    """
    if not failure_counts:
        return "No data found."

    # Sort users alphabetically (optional: sort by count, etc.)
    lines = []
    for user in sorted(failure_counts):
        lines.append(f"{user} – {failure_counts[user]} failed action{'s' if failure_counts[user] != 1 else ''}")
        lines.append("-----")
    # Remove the trailing separator if you don't want an extra line at the end
    if lines and lines[-1] == "-----":
        lines.pop()
    return "\n".join(lines)

    path = Path(csv_file)

"""sentence_truncator.py

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List


class SentenceTruncator:
    """
    Wraps a sentence and offers a ``truncate`` method.

    Parameters
    ----------
    text : str
        The original sentence (or any text) that we want to keep handy.
    """

    __slots__ = ("_text",)

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return self._text

    # Public API
    # --------------------------------------------------------------
    def truncate(self, max_len: int, suffix: str = "...") -> str:
        """
        Return a possibly‑shortened version of the wrapped sentence.

        * If the original text fits into ``max_len`` characters, it is returned
          unchanged (the suffix is **not** added).
        * Otherwise the text is cut so that ``len(result) + len(suffix) <= max_len``.
          The cut never happens in the middle of a word – we keep whole words
          as long as they still fit.  If the very first word is longer than the
          space that is left for content, that word will be truncated.

        Parameters
        ----------
        max_len : int
            The maximum total length *including* the suffix.
        suffix : str, optional
            Text that is appended when truncation occurs.  Defaults to ``"..."``.
            It can be any string (e.g. ``" (more)"``) – the algorithm always
            respects the combined length.

        Returns
        -------
        str
            Either the original sentence (if it already fits) or a truncated
            version with the suffix appended.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If ``max_len`` is not a positive integer or is smaller than the length
            of ``suffix`` (in that case we cannot possibly attach the suffix).

        if max_len <= 0:
            raise ValueError("max_len must be a positive integer")
        if max_len < len(suffix):
            raise ValueError(
                f"max_len ({max_len}) is smaller than the suffix length "
                f"({len(suffix)}); cannot truncate safely."
            )

        # Fast‑path – everything fits, no suffix needed.
        if len(self._text) <= max_len:
            return self._text

        # Space we have for the *content* part (everything before the suffix)
        allowed = max_len - len(suffix)

        words: List[str] = self._text.split()
        kept_words: List[str] = []
        cur_len = 0

        for w in words:
            # +1 accounts for the space that would precede the word

            extra = len(w) if cur_len == 0 else len(w) + 1
            if cur_len + extra > allowed:

        # In that situation we simply slice that word.

        # Normal case – we have at least one whole word.
        result = " ".join(kept_words) + suffix
        return result

        return self._text

Below is a compact, self‑contained Python script that

1. **Consumes** a CSV string (or a file) that contains three columns: `user`, `action`, `outcome`.  
2. **Counts** how many times each user performed a **failed** action (the value of `outcome` is assumed to be the literal word `fail` – you can adapt the test if your data uses a different marker).  
3. **Builds** a human‑readable report where each line looks like:

```
user_name: <failed‑action‑count>
```

   and every line is separated from the next one by a line consisting of 30 dashes (`------------------------------`).  

The final report is a single string that can be printed, written to a file, or returned from a function.

---

## 📦 Complete Code

import csv
import io
from collections import Counter
from typing import Iterable, Tuple, Dict, List


def parse_csv(csv_text: str) -> List[Tuple[str, str, str]]:
    """
    Convert a CSV string into a list of (user, action, outcome) tuples.
    The CSV is expected to have a header row with column names that include
    'user', 'action' and 'outcome' (case‑insensitive). Extra columns are ignored.

    Parameters
    ----------
    csv_text : str
        Whole CSV content as a single string.

    Returns
    -------
    List[Tuple[str, str, str]]
        List of rows, each row being (user, action, outcome).
    """
    # Normalise line endings and create an iterator over lines
    csv_file = io.StringIO(csv_text.strip())
    reader = csv.DictReader(csv_file)

    # Determine column names (case‑insensitive)
    # Store the canonical header names we will use later.
    header_map = {name.lower(): name for name in reader.fieldnames}
    required = ("user", "action", "outcome")
    missing = [c for c in required if c not in header_map]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"CSV is missing required columns: {missing}")

    rows = []
    for line_num, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):          # start=2 → after header
        try:
            user = row[header_map["user"]].strip()
            action = row[header_map["action"]].strip()
            outcome = row[header_map["outcome"]].strip()
            rows.append((user, action, outcome))
        except Exception as exc:
            # You may want to log or collect bad rows instead of aborting.
            raise ValueError(f"Problem parsing line {line_num}: {exc}") from exc
    return rows


def count_failed_actions(
    rows: Iterable[Tuple[str, str, str]],
    fail_marker: str = "fail"
) -> Counter:
    """
    Count how many *failed* actions each user performed.

    Parameters
    ----------
    rows : Iterable[Tuple[user, action, outcome]]
        The rows produced by :func:`parse_csv`.
    fail_marker : str, optional
        Text that marks an outcome as a failure (default: "fail").
        Comparison is case‑insensitive.

    Returns
    -------
    collections.Counter
        Mapping of user → number of failed actions.
    """
    failures = Counter()
    for user, _action, outcome in rows:
        if outcome.lower() == fail_marker.lower():
            failures[user] += 1
    return failures


def build_report(fail_counts: Dict[str, int]) -> str:
    """
    Turn the failure counts into a nicely‑formatted string.

    Each user line is separated from the next by a full line of dashes.

    Example output:

    ```
    alice: 3
    ------------------------------
    bob: 0
    ------------------------------
    ```

    Parameters
    ----------
    fail_counts : Mapping[user, int]
        Result of :func:`count_failed_actions`. Users with a count of 0 can be
        omitted or kept – we keep them for completeness.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        The final report.
    """
    dash_line = "-" * 30
    # Sort for deterministic output (alphabetical by user name)
    sorted_items = sorted(fail_counts.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[0].lower())

    lines: List[str] = []
    for user, cnt in sorted_items:
        lines.append(f"{user}: {cnt}")
        lines.append(dash_line)

    # Remove the trailing dash line for a cleaner looking report
    if lines:
        lines.pop()            # drop the last dashed separator

    return "\n".join(lines)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Convenience wrapper – the single public entry point
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def generate_failure_report(csv_text: str, fail_marker: str = "fail") -> str:
    """
    End‑to‑end helper: parse CSV → count failures → format report.

    Parameters
    ----------
    csv_text : str
        Entire CSV data (including header).
    fail_marker : str, optional
        Text denoting a failure outcome (default: "fail").

    Returns
    -------
    str
        Ready‑to‑print report.
    """
    rows = parse_csv(csv_text)
    fail_counts = count_failed_actions(rows, fail_marker=fail_marker)

    # If you prefer *only* users that actually failed at least once:
    # fail_counts = Counter({u: c for u, c in fail_counts.items() if c > 0})

    return build_report(fail_counts)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example usage (you can delete the block or wrap it under `if __name__ == "__main__":`)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
example_csv = """user,action,outcome,extra_column
alice,login,success,foo
bob,download,fail,bar
alice,upload,fail,baz
charlie,login,success,qux
bob,login,fail,quux
alice,delete,fail,corge
"""

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== Failure Report ===")
    print(generate_failure_report(example_csv))
```

|------|----------|--------------|
| **1️⃣ Parse CSV** | `parse_csv` | Uses `csv.DictReader` → extracts the three needed columns (case‑insensitive) → returns a list of `(user, action, outcome)` tuples. |
| **2️⃣ Count Failures** | `count_failed_actions` | Walks through the rows, increments a `Counter` for every row whose `outcome` matches the *failure marker* (`"fail"` by default). |
| **3️⃣ Build the Report** | `build_report` | Formats each `user: count` line, inserts a line of 30 dashes after every entry, and trims the final separator. Users are sorted alphabetically for reproducibility. |
| **4️⃣ One‑liner Helper** | `generate_failure_report` | Calls the three steps above, returning the final string ready for printing or saving. |

All three logical parts are deliberately **decoupled** so you can reuse them:

* If your CSV lives on disk, simply read it into a string (`open(...).read()`) before passing it to `generate_failure_report`.
* If you need a different failure indicator (e.g., `"error"` or numeric `0`), just set `fail_marker` accordingly.
* If you only want users **with at least one failure**, uncomment the filtering line in `generate_failure_report`.

from collections import Counter
from typing import Iterable, Dict, List


def count_attendance(statuses: Iterable[str]) -> Dict[str, int]:
    """
    Count how many times each attendance status appears in *statuses*.

    Parameters
    ----------
    statuses : iterable of str
        A sequence (list, tuple, generator, …) that contains the raw
        attendance entries.  Expected values are ``"present"``, ``"late"``,
        ``"absent"``, but any string will be counted – the function does not
        enforce a closed set of labels.

    Returns
    -------
    dict
        Mapping ``status -> count``.  Missing statuses are omitted
        (e.g. if there are no “late” entries the returned dict will not have a
        ``"late"`` key).

    Examples
    --------
    >>> records = ["present", "late", "absent", "present", "Late", "PRESENT"]
    >>> count_attendance(records)
    {'present': 2, 'late': 1, 'absent': 1, 'Late': 1, 'PRESENT': 1}
    >>> count_attendance(["present", "present", "absent"])
    {'present': 2, 'absent': 1}
    """
    # The most concise (and fast) way is to hand the iterable to Counter.
    # Counter returns a dict‑like subclass that already maps each unique value
    # to its frequency.
    return dict(Counter(statuses))
```

    return wrap(text, width=width, replace_whitespace=False, drop_whitespace=False)


def format_error(

                      description: str,
                      *,
                      hint: str = "Run '--help' or see the online documentation.") -> str:
    """

    ----------
    error_code:

    description:
        Human‑readable description of what went wrong.

        ``--help`` flag.

    -------
    str

    -------

    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  ERROR E42                                        │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │  Unable to connect to the database.              │
    │                                                   │
    │  Need help? → Run '--help' or see the online ... │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    """
    # ── constants for the box drawing
    H   = "─"
    V   = "│"
    TL  = "┌"
    TR  = "┐"
    BL  = "└"
    BR  = "┘"
    T   = "├"
    B   = "┤"

    # a wider box.  70 characters works nicely for most terminals.
    inner_width = 70

    # Header line
    header = f"ERROR {error_code}"
    header_line = f"{V}  {header:<{inner_width}}{V}"

    # Description – wrap it to *inner_width* and prefix each line with the
    # vertical bar.
    description_lines = [
        f"{V}  {line:<{inner_width}}{V}"
        for line in _wrap_lines(description, width=inner_width)
    ]

    # Blank line separates description from the hint (makes it easier to read)
    blank_line = f"{V}{' ' * (inner_width + 4)}{V}"

    # Hint line – also wrapped; we prepend a friendly “Need help?” prefix.
    hint_prefix = "Need help? → "
    # The first line gets the prefix; the rest are indented.
    wrapped_hint = _wrap_lines(
        hint_prefix + hint,
        width=inner_width
    )
    hint_lines = [

        for line in wrapped_hint
    ]

    middle = f"{T}{H * (inner_width + 4)}{B}"
    bottom = f"{BL}{H * (inner_width + 4)}{BR}"

    parts = [

        header_line,
        middle,
        *description_lines,
        blank_line,
        *hint_lines,
        bottom,
